links.body:
# The Real Story Behind the Bald Knobbers  — Ozarks Alive

**Source:** https://www.ozarksalive.com/stories/the-real-story-behind-the-bald-knobbers

        
          
          
            The Bald Knobbers were vigilantes who operated in Taney, Christian and Douglas counties in the late 1800s.
          
        

The Bald Knobbers rode into a moment of Ozarks history when their presence was needed — or at least its members thought it was. In the 1880s, the uniquely named vigilantes made a name through heavy-handed tactics to maintain law and order and morality as they saw it. Ultimately, they created a lot of strong feelings — and a significant amount of publicity — through newspapers across the country.The first group began in Taney County, Missouri, in 1884 or 1885. Others, including in Douglas and Christian counties, followed. In other places, the Bald Knobbers got credit for work that may or may not have been their doings but were happenings that could be linked to the deeds of vigilantes. But they didn’t last long. By the end of the decade, the two biggest Bald Knobber groups were gone. Taney County’s Bald Knobbers peacefully disbanded after actions by Missouri Governor John S. Marmaduke. The Christian County group went down in a much more dramatic style, with three of its members being hanged on the Ozark square in 1889.“They started as good guys from good families, and they wanted to get things straightened after the Civil War. Everybody did,” said Marie Day, a Christian County historian about what she’d want people to know about the Bald Knobbers. “That was the only way they could figure out how to do it. “It’s like they kind of had a reason for being bad because they had to survive.” Before the Bald Knobbers The Bald Knobbers were one of several vigilante groups in the late 1800s. They were the result of uncertainty and concern in a land still regrouping after the Civil War.“The Civil War led to a surge of lawlessness, both in southwest Missouri and the state at large, and an increased cultural acceptance of violence and vigilantism as a means of solving problems and deterring crime,” wrote Dr. Matthew J. Hernando, author of “Faces Like Devils,” a book about the Bald Knobbers. “Historians have described the post-Civil War period as a ‘reign of terror’ in which former soldiers and guerrillas left the battlefields and faded into Missouri’s countryside only to reemerge later as criminals and outlaws.”The bloody period tore families apart and brought devastation to the region, and the years that followed continued a sense of violence and unrest.“Another condition which permitted outlaws to exist is that during the war the able men were away fighting either because they volunteered or were forced,” notes an article in a 1983 Bittersweet magazine. “Whichever army came through would conscript any men they could find. The women and children and old men were left to live as they could to raise the food for themselves and what stock the maurading armies or outlaws spared them. With law enforcement systems broken down, with alternate periods of Union or Confederate army occupation, men like Alf Bolin and his gang had free sway. The inhabitants lived in constant terror, hiding any older boys or men as well as any livestock from the armies and outlaws.”Bolin was an extreme example, as the notorious outlaw boasted of murdering 40 people (said to be an exaggeration, but you get the idea) before he was killed and beheaded. While people danced in the street when Bolin was killed, it didn’t stop the feeling that crime was out of control. That fear existed in parallel with an influx of newcomers and escalating county debt. “Many felt threatened by their seemingly foreign neighbors and the changes to their way of life that the new socioeconomic order portended,” wrote Hernando. Additionally, he noted, “the Civil War helped create the necessary conditions for groups like the Bald Knobbers to exist by leaving a legacy of bitterness and mistrust between supporters of the Union and the Confederacy.Those realities were kindling a killing set aflame in 1883, when a man named Al Layton was arrested, tried and released for the killing of James “Jim” Everett, a beloved Taney County storekeeper who helped keep families afloat after a drought in 1882.“People were incensed,” wrote Lucile Morris Upton in “Bald Knobbers,” a book published in 1939. “Many of them still owed money, and most of them owed loyalty, to Jim Everett. They said this was another instance in which the courts had failed to punish a Taney County killer. All through that winter men talked in little groups about trying to take the law into their own hands. Often they met behind closed doors in solemn conference. Almost a year wore along, and still men were asking what good citizens should do to insure law and order.”That led to the start of the Bald Knobbers in 1884 or 1885.

![Image 1](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/6191360dc40cc86d79427456/1242ae0a-5093-4899-80af-e81abdddc896/Bald_Knobbers_portray.jpg)

        
          
          
            “Old” Forsyth, where the Taney County Bald Knobbers organized, is now covered by Bull Shoals Lake. (Courtesy of the Johnson Family Collection and Richard Crabtree)
          
        

The group organized in a town that no longer exists – at least in the form it was back then – as it came to be in “old” Forsyth, a town now covered by Bull Shoals Lake. Later they met atop bare hilltops known as “balds,” ultimately earning the Bald Knobber moniker. Their alleged goal was to help maintain law and order. “When we organized, law enforcement hereabouts was broken down,” noted an anonymous source in “Bald Knobbers.” “We met here in Forsyth in the back end of a store building and formed what we then called a citizen’s committee. The members took an oath to see that good officers were elected and to support them.”A key name in the group was Nat Kinney, a larger-than-life saloon operator who fought for the Union in the Civil War. He and his family moved from Springfield to Taney County in 1883. It sounds like the nearly seven-foot-tall Kinney had strong opinions before he moved to the hills, but those came out in greater force as he helped organize locals for causes in which he believed. And those feelings led to action when he felt a force for law and order was needed.He expresses those through a personal statement printed in Upton’s book: “So far as I could learn the history of Taney County has been a record of lawlessness and disregard of social proprieties. When I came here some four years ago (1883) it was common for men to live with women to whom they had never been married. Why, one old Mormonlike neighbor kept six women. Then county was $42,000 in debt, and had not even a plank to show for it. The money had simply been stolen. That wasn’t all. Over thirty men had been shot to death in the county since the war, and not one of the murderers had been punished by the civil authorities.“Well I had come to here to lead a retired and quiet life, but I could not refrain from expressing my opinions of such things and I can not refrain now.”Reign of TerrorThe first reported instance of the Bald-Knobbers-involved doings was in April 1885, when the group was allegedly involved with lynching — hanging without legal process — two men. Frank and Tubal Taylor had shot a storekeeper and his wife; locals believed that justice would not be served, so they took matters into their own hands.“So many lawbreakers had gotten off scott-free for 20, 25 years after the Civil War that they weren’t really concerned,” said Curtis Copeland, leader of the Society of Ozarkian Hillcrofters, a preservation group he helped revive and a local Bald Knobber expert. “They were ready to bond out. Before they could get bonded out, a lynch mob formed, which was basically Bald Knobbers, and they hung them. “That’s when everybody’s like, ‘Sure, this might have been a law-and-order thing, but this is just too far.’ It just escalated from there. Very quickly, the whole county, you were either for them or against them. There wasn’t really any middle ground.” It didn’t take long before there was opposition to the group. In early 1885 – around the time of those first hangings – a group called the Anti-Bald Knobbers also organized. 

![Image 2](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/6191360dc40cc86d79427456/4a6aa0bc-3a13-4658-b7cb-6266d4077402/467512589_10230570043649110_5220877515762676032_n.jpg)

        
          
          
            Shortly after the Bald Knobbers organized, an opposition group — the Anti-Bald Knobbers — also formed. (Courtesy the Kansas City Times)
          
        
      
        
      

    “A lot of what would become the Anti-Bald Knobbers were residents of Taney County well before the Civil War,” Copeland said. “So they had a little of pushback about the ‘newcomer’ type of thing.” That opposition didn’t stop the group’s actions, which quickly escalated through word and deed. They exercised their own form of justice across the county, leading some papers to print when someone they wrote about in Taney County was not a Bald Knobber.“Taney County is making herself a most unenviable record, and it appears that her example in mob violence is spreading over the entire southwest,” noted the Pineville News in August 1885.According to the Jefferson City Tribune in November 1885, the Bald Knobbers told some families they had to leave the county – which they did. They told Jerome Winslow to leave because he talked too much and was a friend of the Taylors, the men who the group had lynched a few months prior. They told a man he had to move a fence because it was in their way. He chose not to, so they pushed it down. They arrested two young men “who refused to surrender to about forty of them.” The pair were taken without warrant to a magistrate who fined them $25 for carrying concealed weapons. “The father of these boys is one of the best citizens of the county and has been for years treasurer of the Masonic lodge of the county,” the paper continued. “He intends to leave as soon as his affairs are fixed up. The justice of Oliver township left the county and moved to Lawrence County. He could do no business. He was not a Bald Knobber.“Jefferson Weaver, son-in-law of ex-Sheriff Moseby, was ordered away, so he may not be present as a witness in a case of felonious assault in which one of the Knobbers was a defendant. These are only a few of the many cases of personal injury charged to these regulators.” In 1886, about 75 Bald Knobbers allegedly rode into Ava “and read the citizens and officers a lecture, then fired a couple of shots into a lawyers office and cautioned the editors of the Record about what they published in their paper. (“The next week the editors of the Record gave them to understand that they would print whatever they saw fit, and take care of themselves, and it is very likely the B.K.’s will give the Record office a wide berth the next time they come to town.”) Later that year, some 50 horsemen rode into Marshfield. “They are supposed to be ‘bald-knobbers,’ as they posted a notice on the court house door requesting witnesses to testify to the truth and referring them to the ten commandments,” noted the Springfield Daily Leader in September 1886. “No one was harmed. They are supposed to be the same gang who cut off the whiskers of the justice of the peace at Seymour recently.”Expansion beyond Taney CountyPapers gave the Bald Knobbers considerable publicity, most assuredly raising public awareness, and an interest grew in other places about similar efforts. Some vigilante efforts in other Ozarks counties were attributed or linked in some way to the Bald Knobbers. Perhaps there were self-described groups, or others labeled unfortunate realities as the work of the Bald Knobbers when there wasn’t any connection. “We're talking about an era where there's a lot of vigilante activity,” Copeland said. “It's kind of the classic Bonnie and Clyde or Jesse James type of thing, where a lot of times a group or individuals get saddled with a criminal act or something that they didn't necessarily do.”But in at least two Ozarks counties – Douglas and Christian – there were verified Bald Knobbers. Some of the previously described Bald Knobber actions may have been through one of those groups. The Douglas County group pulled from close to the Webster County line, I’ve been told. Stories of that group have been heard by folks like Cinita Brown, now 94, whose late husband’s grandfather was involved in some way with the local knobbers. “I knew of a family in Douglas County,” she said. “The husband had been older than the wife and they married, and she had a little boy. Then when he was very small, she died. Of course, he couldn’t take care of the child so he hired a girl to come and take care of the little boy. “She actually was abusing the little boy – just physically abusing him, and emotionally abusing him. The little boy got old enough to tell some people. Different people kept hearing this same story from the little boy. “So the story kept being repeated and finally they (the Bald Knobbers) got together and got their uniforms on and went to the house with a bundle of switches tied together. They knocked on the door and she came to the door and they left the switches and said, ‘Tonight we’re leaving them. … If we ever hear one more story about how you take care of little Johnny, we will be back.’ She went ahead and left the country. That was a known story.” Christian County’s group was organized in 1885, following a markedly different track from the original group. Taney County Bald Knobbers were focused on law and order, while Christian County were more focused on morality – a reality that appears linked to places like Chadwick, which today is a sleepy village but in that era was a boomtown tied to the railroad, complete with saloons and brothels. 

![Image 3](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/6191360dc40cc86d79427456/20a3a0f1-3e3c-4851-be9f-9ab838abb76d/Bald_Knobbers.jpg)

        
          
          
            Chadwick, Missouri, is shown in 2025.
          
        
      
        
      

    “You have all these sustenance farmers that were just trying to make a living, and all of a sudden had this new income,” Copeland said. “So with income comes the folks that want to get that money. You start to get your vice, and pretty soon Chadwick was a very rowdy town of gambling, alcohol, all that stuff.”And so the Bald Knobbers became the Morality Police. “The Bald Knobbers paid our town another visit last night about 1 o’clock,” noted the Pineville News, reporting a Chadwick dispatch, in November 1886. “They came for the purpose of raiding the saloons, pouring out the whiskey and ordering the saloon keepers to leave town within five days. They went deliberately to work to carry out their purpose by opening the faucets, driving in the heads of the barrels, emptying the bottles, etc.”

![Image 4](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/6191360dc40cc86d79427456/3a57f462-64f6-4f8c-af14-03b1aa6b98b2/DSC_5751.JPG)

        
          
          
            A replica of the Christian County Bald Knobber mask is on display at the Chadwick Museum.
          
        

It’s the Chadwick group that is tied to the Bald Knobber’s distinctive mask: A black face and head covering complete with horns.“What really also set them apart was they had a brand — and that brand was the Christian County Bald Knobbers’ masks,” Copeland said.“Whether they knew it or not at the time, they had a brand and that carried on.”The Demise of the Bald KnobbersUntil they didn’t. From high places to low drops, the Bald Knobbers came to dramatic ends in different ways.The Taney County group officially ended in 1886 after intervention from Missouri leaders. “General Jamison, after a thorough examination of the case, taking evidence from both of the factions, called a meeting and gave the leaders of each side good advice,” noted the Tribune. “He told them that there were times when a vigilance committee filled a want, but the perpetuation of such an organization was hurtful to any community. It was wrong for any body of men to take the law into their own hands, and it always resulted in evil. “The meeting and the talk of General Jamison had the effect of harmonizing the factions and allaying the bitter feeling which has existed for years in Taney County, and the day after the general left the Bald Knobbers held a meeting, the proceedings of which were mailed to him…”Those proceedings decreed that the “organization of the citizens’ committee be disbanded.” Another article noted that, “The peace and prosperity of the county is now permanently assured, which, added to the fact that valuable lead mines have been discovered on Secretary of State McGrath’s farm, is certain to bring Taney County up to the standard of a majority of the counties in the state.” Some doubted whether the group had actually disbanded or simply said it had. But the Christian County Bald Knobbers were still active at this time; their presence was not part of the supposed capitulation. 

![Image 5](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/6191360dc40cc86d79427456/763189ef-99bc-4193-98c6-b6f67238a25f/515507053_1440180070959426_6814691337476610301_n.jpg)

        
          
          
            St. Louis Post-Dispatch; May 10, 1889
          
        
      
        
      

    It wasn’t too long, however, before they came to an end (on paper) in very dramatic fashion as well. Steps to that reality were set in motion in 1887, when the group met what was known as Smelter Holler near Sparta and Chadwick. Its leader was a man named Dave Walker, born in 1847 in Kentucky before coming to the Ozarks.“The men present discussed a variety of topics, much of it unrelated to any kind of vigilante business,” wrote Hernando in “Faces Like Devils.” “Gilbert Applegate recalled that they talked about ‘shooting, and making ties, and so-on … and bragging on their guns and one thing and another.’ Some of the men suggested whipping various individuals, but most of those present rejected these proposals. Then someone proposed that they go pour out some whiskey belonging to a local moonshiner named William (“Bucky Bill”) Roberts, to which Dave Walker agreed.” That is where the plan when awry. Because as the group departed, some of them split off when they realized how close they were to William Edens’ cabin. The man had insulted them, and they decided it would be a good opportunity to pay him a visit. “The Edens family was recognized as honorable and upright. But the men were tie hackers with independence and the masked band continued to hold that against them. There was a story also that further fuel was heaped on the enmity when either Charles Green or the younger Edens had shot and killed a dog with a rifle while hauling timber to Sparta. He wisecracked that he had ‘killed a Bald Knobber.’ To compare a person to a dog always was an opening for a fight in the hills.”Dave Walker called the men back. But whether they didn’t hear him or they chose not to listen, it did no good. Even after the group reached the cabin and found it empty, their momentum took them to Edens’ father’s house, where a bloody ambush resulted in William Edens and Charles Greene dead.Aftermath of the Murders

![Image 6](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/6191360dc40cc86d79427456/4a112b4f-7521-40ca-8fdd-19124f909bba/Screenshot+2025-08-13+at+7.12.00%E2%80%AFPM.png)

        
          
          
            A newspaper sketch depicts the Christian County Bald Knobbers’ raid on the Edens cabin. (Courtesy of the St. Louis Post-Dispatch)
          
        
      
        
      

    Prior to the Greene-Edens murders, there was a growing level of opposition to the group but their actions didn’t prompt much action from local law enforcement. The murders changed that reality.  “The tragic events that took place inside James Edens’s cabin lasted only a few minutes, but they fundamentally altered the entire course of the Bald Knobber movement,” wrote Hernando. “Overnight the vigilantes had transformed themselves from righteous defenders of law and Christian morality into murderers, outlaws and social pariahs, an outcome that surely surprised many of them.”Christian County Sheriff Zachariah Johnson was responsible for finding the men suspected of the crimes. After locating Bald Knobber Joe Inman, the sheriff received a confession and information that led him to others who were said to be involved, ultimately rounding up 25 people in about a week. Later, a complicated ruse led to the capture of William Walker, who had escaped to Arkansas with the aid of family despite a leg being injured in the shootout. The men were eventually taken to Springfield, where the jail was more secure. After the construction of the “Bald Knobber Jail,” as a brick building on the Ozark square came to be known, they were returned to Ozark.“They also deputized many local residents of Ozark and the surrounding area to assist law enforcement officials in providing security,” penned Hernando. “Years later one such resident, Andrew Jackson Whitehead, recalled that local authorities deputized around 100 men to serve as guards at the jail because they believed that ‘some organized effort might be made by the Bald Knobbers to rescue the four condemned men.”The confinement of so many men led to challenges for their families, and at one point several were camped near the courthouse. The Springfield Republican noted that there were about 30 people in the camp, a group that included the wives of about a dozen Bald Knobbers. “Many of these women have found it very difficult to make both ends meet since the 15th of last March, when their husbands, fathers, brothers or sons, as the case may be, were arrested,” the paper noted. “Mrs. Elizabeth Mathews and Mrs. Rachel Mathews and two or three others have been obliged to cut ties and posts and do other heavy work, fitted only for the brawny arms of men. “‘We have just had to do it or starve,’ said Mrs. Elizabeth Mathews. ‘Even then part of the time we were on half rations. Very few of us have any homes, and we have to do any sort of work. Rachel can make eight or ten ties a day, but lots of times they’d cull out half of them; so you see there’s mighty little money in it.’ Gradually, many of the arrested men gave confessions, leaving four to pay for the crime: “Bull Creek” Dave Walker; William Walker, his son; John Matthews; and Wiley Matthews, his nephew. They were sentenced to hang, but remained in jail as the case was appealed. 

![Image 7](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/6191360dc40cc86d79427456/c2c08b57-fe12-4b7c-8bcb-abcbfd67e9ff/Screenshot+2025-08-13+at+6.15.50%E2%80%AFPM.png)

        
          
          
            A jail was built in Ozark to house the Bald Knobbers. It was torn down in 1929. (Clipping courtesy of Wayne Glenn)
          
        

At least some of them did. The Matthewses ultimately broke through a wall of the jail and escaped in December 1888. John Matthews was captured and returned to jail, while lore says that Wiley Matthews headed for Oklahoma. He was never recaptured. The Walkers chose not to escape.But let’s go back to Taney County for just a moment. A few months earlier, another Bald Knobber met his end: Nat Kinney, leader of the Taney County group, was shot and killed by anti-Bald Knobber William (Billy) Miles.“From 1884 to the breaking up of the Bald Knob gang, Kinney was king of the boldest band of outlaws that ever disgraced the Southwest,” noted the Joplin Herald in 1888. The story was published in many papers across the state. “His first individual murder was the killing of Andrew Cogburn at a church near Ozark on Sunday, March 12, 1886. After this numerous outrages were charged to him and his death is hailed with as much joy by the anti-Knobbers as it is with the frenzied sorrow by members of the old band.”The trouble escalated the following year, when Sheriff Branson was also killed by Miles.“Three hundred armed men are out day and night hunting William Mil(es), who killed Sheriff Br(a)nson, of Taney County, on the 4th of July,” noted the Kansas City Journal in July 1889. “The people all seem to think that the trouble has just commenced and the old grudges that existed between the Bald Knobbers and anti-Baldknobbers will be taken up again and Taney Countians will again take up arms against one another and have a war between themselves.”The Bald Knobber HangingsBack in Ozark, by the time this article was printed, the Walkers and John Matthews were dead. They were hanged in May 1889 on the Ozark square.Newspapers account the hours before the hanging. The elder Walker was resigned to his fate, while John Matthews voiced his innocence until the end. In the hours before the three men were led from the jail, William Walker decided he wanted to be baptized. “An ordinary bath tub was taken into the jail and filled with water and everything ready for immersion,” noted the Springfield Leader. When the minister asked to perform the ritual didn’t arrive, “Rev. Mr. Horn of the M.E. church, South, and Rev. Mr. Grayson of the Missionary Baptists, performing the ceremonies, during which the Walkers and John Matthews prayed with earnestness and fervor.” Religious services were held that night, continuing until 10 p.m. “The Walkers maintained the same fortitude that has characterized them throughout the ordeal but Matthews gives way to grief and repining, the paper continued. “They all maintain innocence of intention of committing murder when they went to the house of Edens, but refuse all efforts to induce them to make confession or statements.”The night was lit by a bright full moon, the paper noted. The next morning, people began arriving – but not, the paper noted, all that many from Christian County. By then, reports note many locals’ opinions had softened on the situation. And for others, it was personal. “A few days before the execution, Mr. Johnson (Christian County sheriff) went to the doomed men and told them he was going to employ a man from St. Louis to act as hangman in his stead as he had been a lifelong friend of the prisoners and that it was more than he could stand to place the noose around their necks,” noted the Ralls County Record in March 1913. The prisoners refused that idea. 

![Image 8](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/6191360dc40cc86d79427456/aca784f1-d655-40e1-a71c-5941b0bde1a4/466387619_9373323932700807_3691590919215166601_n.jpg)

        
          
          
            A marker once stood on the Ozark square to mark where the Bald Knobbers were hanged in 1889. (Courtesy of Missouri State University Libraries)
          
        
      
        
      

    At approximately 9:35 a.m., the men were escorted to the gallows. “The two Walkers stepped firmly, calmly, resolutely – Mathews lingered on the steps and exhorted the beholders to act and walk in the light of God and avoid evil associates which had brought him to this,” noted the Leader. “Prayers were offered and hymns were sung in which the condemned joined.” The hanging killed the elder Walker and Mathews quickly. However, William Walker did not transition easily.The rope with which he was hanged stretched when he dropped, resulting in his feet touching on the ground and the noose partially slipping off his head. He was hanged a second time. “The accident that befell William Walker could not be attributed to Sheriff Johnson, who took all human precaution but not being a professional hangman he could not be expected to be perfect. It is a strong argument in favor of the bill now pending in the legislature requiring all executions to be in the State penitentiary.” Aftermath Even though the groups in Taney and Christian counties formally ended by 1890, there are reports of Bald Knobber activities occurring later than that time. One example is in Douglas County, where Copeland recalls a man he knew in the 1970s, then in his 80s. Originally from western Douglas County, the man was well aware of Bald Knobber activities. “I said, ‘Have you ever heard of the Bald Knobbers?’ He was like, ‘Oh yeah — they were doing their thing well into the 1920s.’”Regardless of activities, the Bald Knobbers found a couple of PR boosts in the first third of the 20th century through “The Shepherd of the Hills,” a novel by Harold Bell Wright, that was published in 1907.  

![Image 9](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/6191360dc40cc86d79427456/a4f8db85-362c-48b5-98e6-18273a6e97d7/Rafferty_23_full.jpg)

        
          
          
            Visitors still come to Old Matt’s Cabin, a location in “The Shepherd of the Hills.” 
          
        
      
        
      

    They also appeared in a lost version of a film by the same name in 1913. The film was extremely controversial, and bans were attempted in Springfield by the local censorship board. Feelings were so strong by some that the creator was actually arrested (and later released). “The board of censors … were of the unanimous opinion tha tthe pictures, in their delineation of outlawry, cruelty and lawlessness would have a harmful effect on the young people of the city,” noted the Springfield Republican in June 1913. “The censors also believed that the pictures would give Missouri and the Ozarks a great deal of unfavorable advertising, and should be suppressed for that reason, if no other.”As of 2025, it’s presumed that the films have been lost to time. Attorney W.L. Vandeventer wrote about the vigilantes. But another big literary moment was in 1939, when Lucile Morris Upton’s “Bald Knobbers” book was published. The book by the local journalist represented 15 years of work and interviews – with primary sources who recalled that era firsthand – and was not told so much as a history book but as a novel that told the story in an engaging way. 

![Image 10](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/6191360dc40cc86d79427456/f1f740d4-2c94-4648-ab09-7b6fd0119ebf/Shepherd+of+the+Hills.jpg)

        
          
          
            Lucile Morris Upton is shown with Mary Elizabeth Mahnkey, a well-known Ozarks poet whose father, Alanzo Prather, was a Bald Knobber. (Courtesy of the Springfield-Greene County Library District)
          
        
      
        
      

    “That turbulent story is one to which I have devoted sincere effort in the search for accuracy,” Upton wrote in the book’s foreword. “Some pioneers will disagree with bits of the story as I have related it. To them I can only reply that I have done my best to discover all versions and choose the one which appeared true.“The old timers also hold few hatreds. Most of them do not like to talk of the turbulent times when night riders lighted their signal fires on high bald peaks. That is due more to the misunderstanding with which the world has looked upon the Bald Knobbers than to any apology the survivors hold for connection with the organization.” Some 20 years later, the Baldknobbers music group debuted in Branson. They chose their moniker not because of any ties with the vigilantes, but because of its local recognition through “The Shepherd of the Hills.” “Lots of people read the book,” Bob Mabe, one of the group’s founding members, said in an oral history interview in 2018. “I just chose the name ‘Baldknobbers’ because of that. We weren’t vigilantes – we were just musicians.” 

        
          
          
            White River Leader; May 18, 1962
          
        
      
        
      

    Bald Knobbers were also featured in “Fire In The Hole,” a well-known amusement ride at Silver Dollar City. The ride, which was replaced in 2024, still features versions of the vigilantes.  And, in 2017, another film was officially complete. This one, however, was not lost to time. “Baldknobber” premiered after years of work, many local folks’ involvement and shooting across the region, including some of the sites where Bald Knobber activities actually took place. Copeland was involved with that film as a cast member as well as in writing. A key takeaway: Feelings are still strong. “The thing about it is — there are still people who have the sentiments and people who still feel strongly about which side they were on,” Copeland said.An example is over in Christian County, where a few years ago I visited with David House, who is related to David and William Walker, two of the condemned Bald Knobbers.“My name is William David House. I'm named after these guys,” he said. “I think David Walker’s brother Gatson Walker – Gat Walker – would have been the lineage that I come directly from on my mother’s side. My mother’s maiden name was Walker.”We drove along to see landmarks that join our world with that of the Bald Knobbers (some of which are on private property, so please do not trespass). One is the cave where the group met that’s between Chadwick and Sparta.“See where these trees are at, where this hollow is? You go right down in there and there is a bluff with a very small cave on it,” he told me. “And they met at kind of a little hollow there.” Another is the Fairview Church, close to where a cabin once stood that was important in Walker family lore. “When I was a boy, my grandfather – Lloyd Walker – and I were squirrel hunting out here,” Walker said. “He took me to some fallen-down remnants of what had been a cabin. I doubt if I could even find it now if it was still there. But he pointed it out to me and said, ‘This is where the sheriff came to arrest Uncle David.’” Land on Fairview Ridge in general is a pain point for the family. “From what I understand, the lawyer they hired to represent both of them at the murder trial – they had agreed to sign off the land that was out here in the Fairview Ridge,” House said. “I think David Walker’s wife and the remainder of the children were allowed to live there, but the attorney owned the property thereafter. “I would say it caused quite a bit of hardship for them. Of course, there was the stigma that she was the widow of an executed murderer, even though (he wasn’t there). Having children of my own, I can’t imagine how it would be to know that one of my children had been executed.”And then there’s the cemeteries where John Matthews and the Walkers are buried. The latter two are in Sparta, tucked unassumingly near the intersection of Highway 125 and 14 in the small Christian County town. History is close. Folks like Marie Day know this, too. The nearly 90-year-old Christian County historian said that when she began conducting research years ago, folks didn’t want to talk about the Bald Knobbers at all. Tensions, even years later, were too hot. “I talked to different people for stories, and I said, ‘OK, what about the Bald Knobbers?’ Most of them wouldn’t even talk about them. And that was in 1983,” said Marie Day, the Christian County historian. “It was too sensitive at that time. They just didn’t talk about them.”Resources“Alf Bolin: Just the Facts, Part II,” Larry Wood, Missouri and Ozarks History, accessed Aug. 11, 2025”Bald Knobber,” Lucile Morris Upton, 1939 “Bald-Knobbers” at Marshfield,” Springfield Daily Leader, Sept. 22, 1886“Bald Knobbers visit Chadwick, Mo.” Pineville News, Nov. 10, 1886“Captain Kinney did not organization Bald Knobbers,” Floyd Sullivan, Springfield Press, Aug. 16, 1930”Captain of Bald Knobbers breaks long silence,” Springfield Press, March 15, 1930“Had a good effect,” The Daily Tribune, April 14, 1886“Hanged!” The Springfield Leader, May 16, 1889”Kinney Killed,” Joplin Herald, Aug. 23, 1888”Laid to Anti-Bald-Knobbers,” Kansas City Times, Dec. 15, 1886No headline, Lexington Register, April 23, 1885No headline, Pineville News, Aug. 26, 1885No headline, The State Journal, April 9, 1886No headline, The Daily Tribune, April 23, 1886”Old jail where three ‘Bald Knobbers’ were hanged in 1889 to be torn down,” Unterrified Democrat, Feb. 21, 1929”Ozark bandit scenes make more trouble,” Springfield Republican, June 27, 1913“The pathetic side,” Springfield Republican, Aug. 25, 1887”Recalls days of Bald Knobbers,” Ralls County Record, March 21, 1913“Who the heck was Alf Bolin?,” Vickie Hooper, Bittersweet, Spring 1983 “W.L. links.title: Freewrite || A Small Beginning
links.body:
![PSX_20260603_080701.jpg](https://images.hive.blog/DQmTwmzAsPnNUX4AHXny5Ncu4kpXRTiPa6eYupzbQd4G4oZ/PSX_20260603_080701.jpg)
![hive dividers-04.png](https://images.hive.blog/DQmdvc788wxsBSQHY3z21o3wSTU7hqRnyYc2JFEn2pEYSev/hive%20dividers-04.png)
Today I noticed something very interesting while walking around the garden. Among the dry leaves, pieces of old branches, and dusty soil, a tiny green shoot had emerged from the ground. It was still very small, but its fresh green color stood out clearly against the brown surroundings.

Looking at it reminded me that every great thing begins with a small step. This little sprout is still fragile and vulnerable, yet it has the courage to push through the soil and reach for the sunlight. Nature always has a way of teaching valuable lessons without saying a single word.

The environment around the sprout was not perfect. The ground looked dry, and there were many obstacles scattered around it. Even so, the young plant continued to grow. It did not wait for ideal conditions before starting its journey. Instead, it simply began with what was available.

In many ways, life is similar. Sometimes we postpone our goals because we feel unprepared or because circumstances are not exactly as we wish. However, progress often starts when we decide to move forward despite limitations. Just like this tiny plant, growth happens little by little each day.

Seeing this small sign of life brought a sense of hope and optimism. With proper care, sunlight, and water, it may eventually become a strong and healthy plant. For now, it serves as a reminder that every achievement starts from a humble beginning.

Thank you for reading my freewrite today. May we continue growing, learning, and moving forward one small step at a time.

links.title: Cabeza de gallo | Enzalada tradicional del amazonas venezolano [ES][EN]
links.body:
> Hace un tiempo atrás, preparé una ensalada de yuca típica de los estados llaneros de Venezuela. Esa ensalada fue toda una experiencia y una forma de entender que la yuca se adapta muy bien como ingrediente. Esta vez me voy al Amazonas venezolano y preparo una ensalada que tiene como base el mañoco, que es una harina o especie de cereal que se prepara con la yuca amarga. Esta ensalada es totalmente diferente a la ensalada de yuca de los llanos, pero se ha convertido en una de mis ensaladas favoritas. > A while back, I made a cassava salad typical of Venezuela’s Llanos region. That salad was quite an experience and helped me realize just how versatile cassava is as an ingredient. This time, I’m heading to the Venezuelan Amazon to make a salad based on mañoco, which is a flour or type of cereal made from bitter cassava. This salad is completely different from the cassava salad from the plains, but it has become one of my favorites. ![1000262260.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/josecarrerag/1000262260.jpg) El mañoco tiene un aroma y sabor que me encanta. A pesar de ser un producto derivado de la yuca, no es que tenga un sabor específico a yuca. El mañoco se debe hidratar y es una ventaja, ya que se puede hidratar con el jugo de los vegetales, jugo de limón o agua, dependiendo de los gustos que se deseen en la ensalada. Puedes agregar más vegetales de los que ves en la lista de ingredientes o menos; eso va a depender de tus gustos. > I love the aroma and flavor of mañoco. Even though it’s made from cassava, it doesn’t really taste like cassava. Mañoco needs to be rehydrated, which is a plus, since you can do so using vegetable juice, lemon juice, or water, depending on the flavors you want in your salad. You can add more or fewer vegetables than those listed in the ingredients; it all depends on your personal taste. ![1000262262.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/josecarrerag/1000262262.jpg) ![1000262261.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/josecarrerag/1000262261.jpg) Esta ensalada me encanta, ya que te hace evitar el tener que agregar carbohidratos a un plato por estar presente el mañoco. Yo preparé unas chuletas y el acompañante fue esta ensalada cabeza de gallo. También no está presente el tema del gluten y, por la alta concentración de fibra, termina siendo un gusto digestivo. Se puede preparar para acompañar pescado frito, milanesas de pollo o simplemente comerla sola. > I love this salad because the manioc means you don’t have to add extra carbs to your meal. I made some pork chops and served them with this cabeza de gallo salad. It’s also gluten-free, and thanks to its high fiber content, it’s easy on the stomach. You can serve it with fried fish, breaded chicken cutlets, or just eat it on its own. ![1000262263.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/josecarrerag/1000262263.jpg) Si quieres aprender a preparar esta versión de la cabeza de gallo, estos son los ingredientes que yo utilicé:  > If you want to learn how to make this version of cabeza de gallo, here are the ingredients I used: ![17338874770083186545070987094077.png](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/josecarrerag/246bKsfbzTQeu6kJmETVNgqsUaKD5PEoEr7VWZd7KJ2ZJPMVRQvdgnHyzwiAnrKsjBdtb.png)

Ingredientes || Ingredients

- 150gr de mañoco - 4-5 limones - 1 ají picante - 1 ají dulce - 2 tomates - 1 rama de cebollín  - Cilantro al gusto - Perejil al gusto - 2 cucharadas de aceite - Sal y pimienta negra al gusto - 150 g of mañoco - 4–5 limes - 1 hot chili pepper - 1 sweet chili pepper - 2 tomatoes - 1 bunch of scallions - Cilantro to taste - Parsley to taste - 2 tablespoons of oil - Salt and black pepper to taste
![17338874770083186545070987094077.png](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/josecarrerag/246bKsfbzTQeu6kJmETVNgqsUaKD5PEoEr7VWZd7KJ2ZJPMVRQvdgnHyzwiAnrKsjBdtb.png)

Preparación || Preparation

- Lo primero es hidratar el mañoco. Yo exprimo jugo de limón en un poco de agua y agrego esa especie de limonada sobre el mañoco. La idea es que el agua apenas sobrepase la cantidad de mañoco. Se deja reposar unos 5 minutos; vas a notar que el mañoco triplica el tamaño. > - The first step is to soak the mañoco. I squeeze some lemon juice into a little water and pour this lemonade-like mixture over the manioc. The idea is for the water to just barely cover the manioc. Let it sit for about 5 minutes; you’ll notice that the manioc triples in size. ![1000262258.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/josecarrerag/1000262258.jpg) - Se cortan los tomates en cuadritos, los ajíes en cuadritos y todos los demás vegetales bien picaditos. Se agregan al mañoco, junto con sal y pimienta, y se mezcla todo muy bien. Se agrega extra de limón al gusto; la idea es que quede un sabor ácido agradable. Se agrega el aceite y, una vez esté todo mezclado, se deja reposar unos 5-10 minutos para que el mañoco siga absorbiendo todos los sabores. Una vez listo, servir a gusto. > - Dice the tomatoes and chili peppers, and finely chop all the other vegetables. Add them to the mañoco, along with salt and pepper, and mix everything thoroughly. Add extra lime juice to taste; the goal is to achieve a pleasant tangy flavor. Add the oil, and once everything is mixed, let it sit for about 5–10 minutes so the mañoco can continue to absorb all the flavors. Once ready, serve as desired. ![1000262259.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/josecarrerag/1000262259.jpg) Ya la cabeza de gallo está lista. Esta ensalada es muy fresca en sabores y muy agradable en textura. Me encanta el carácter del ají combinado con el limón. Una vez que se prepara este tipo de ensaladas, se vuelve un vicio comerlas porque aportan mucho y eliminan esa necesidad de agregar ciertos carbohidratos a las comidas que suelen llevar mucho tiempo de cocción y que no terminan siendo tan buenos para la salud. > The cabeza de gallo is ready. This salad has a very fresh flavor and a pleasant texture. I love the way the chili pepper pairs with the lemon. Once you start making salads like this, it becomes hard to stop—they’re so satisfying and eliminate the need to add certain carbohydrates to meals that usually take a long time to cook and aren’t all that healthy. ![1000262264.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/josecarrerag/1000262264.jpg) Déjame saber en los comentarios si antes habías comido mañoco y cuál fue tu experiencia. ¡Hasta una próxima receta! > Let me know in the comments if you've ever tried mañoco before and what your experience was like. See you next recipe! --- ---

links.title: Nosferatu — Old Shadows That Still Know How to Move
links.body:
![Nosferatu public domain frame](https://archive.org/download/nosferatu_1922/__ia_thumb.jpg)

# Nosferatu — Old Shadows That Still Know How to Move

Some horror films become old in the wrong way. The effects start to show, the rhythm feels trapped in another century, and the fear turns into a museum object. **Nosferatu** is old, of course, but it has not gone quiet. It still has that thin, cold feeling of something watching from the corner of the room.

Official/public-domain viewing link: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FC6jFoYm3xs

![Nosferatu still](https://archive.org/download/nosferatu_1922/nosferatu_1922.thumbs/nosferatu_1922_000594.jpg)

## Why I chose it today

After writing about a song last time, I wanted to return to cinema with something that has a different kind of energy. Not a new release. Not a loud franchise piece. Something slower, stranger, and more skeletal.

F. W. Murnau's 1922 silent film is often discussed as an unofficial Dracula adaptation, with names changed and the story reshaped. That legal shadow is part of its history, but the film survives for a better reason: Count Orlok does not feel like a normal screen vampire. He feels like illness, obsession, bad dreams, and empty streets given a body.

## The story in simple shape

The plot is direct. A young real-estate clerk travels to a remote castle to arrange a property sale. The client, Count Orlok, is not merely eccentric. He is something older and hungrier. Once Orlok sees the clerk's wife through a portrait and decides to move closer to her town, the film shifts from private danger to public dread.

That is one of the strongest parts of the movie. It is not only about one victim or one haunted house. The horror travels. It arrives by ship. It enters a community. It spreads through rumor, silence, coffins, and fear.

![Nosferatu castle/travel still](https://archive.org/download/nosferatu_1922/nosferatu_1922.thumbs/nosferatu_1922_001914.jpg)

## Orlok still works

Max Schreck's Count Orlok is not romantic. That matters. Many later vampires became smooth, beautiful, tragic, or seductive. Orlok is not built that way. His face is narrow, his fingers look too long, and his movements have a stiff, insect-like patience.

He does not need many gestures. A doorway, a staircase, a shadow on a wall — the film knows how to make him disturbing with very little. That restraint is why some images remain powerful even now. The famous shadow is not just a trick shot. It turns the monster into a shape, almost an idea, moving toward the victim before the body fully arrives.

## The silence helps

Silent cinema can feel distant if someone expects modern pacing. Here, the silence becomes part of the pressure. The faces, cards, architecture, and body language do more work. Because there is no spoken dialogue, every room feels a little more exposed.

I also like how the film uses daylight. It is not only a night-world. Some of the most uneasy moments happen in bright spaces, which makes the danger feel less like a ghost story and more like a sickness crossing into normal life.

![Nosferatu still from archive](https://archive.org/download/nosferatu_1922/nosferatu_1922.thumbs/nosferatu_1922_003294.jpg)

## What feels dated

The acting style is broad compared with modern film. Some reactions are theatrical, and a few transitions can feel abrupt. Anyone coming from current horror may need a few minutes to adjust to the rhythm.

But I do not see that as a real weakness. It is part of the grammar of the period. Once the eye accepts it, the film becomes easier to read. The exaggeration is not random; it points the viewer toward emotion, danger, and moral panic.

## What still feels fresh

The best thing about **Nosferatu** is its atmosphere. It understands that horror is not only a monster appearing. Horror is waiting. Horror is the road to the castle. Horror is the ship arriving with no comfort left inside it. Horror is a town slowly realizing that something has entered and normal explanations are too small.

That feeling is still useful today. Modern horror often has more sound, more editing, more blood, and more explanation. This film has less, but sometimes less leaves more space for the mind to participate.

![Nosferatu public domain still](https://archive.org/download/nosferatu_1922/nosferatu_1922.thumbs/nosferatu_1922_004974.jpg)

## Final thoughts

**Nosferatu** is not scary in the same way a modern jump-scare film is scary. It is thinner, colder, and more patient. It works like a bad memory from a time before horror had fixed rules.

For me, that is the reason it remains worth discussing. It is not just an important old title people mention out of respect. It is still a film with images that can disturb the room around you. Count Orlok walks slowly, but the shadow he leaves behind is fast.

Image/source note: stills are from the public-domain Internet Archive copy of *Nosferatu* (1922).

links.title: Has the art of thinking been lost?
links.body: <center>[Forbes](https://www.forbes.com/sites/alexanderpuutio/2025/11/12/from-systems-of-record-to-systems-of-reason-the-enterprise-ai-revolution/)</center>\nWhen we talk about human evolution, anyone who dares to question this fact is signing a certificate of immense stupidity and ignorance. Indeed, human evolution has happened. However, it is necessary to pay attention to another point: how far has this evolution managed to go after so many years? I know that effective answers to this cannot be found anywhere, but there is no harm in \

to understand where we are.\nThis text came to mind (earlier) after I watched a television commercial talking about the power of digital influencers in today's society. The focus of the commercial was not, however, to talk about how digital influencers do this; but rather, to provoke the viewer about the art of thinking through critical thinking about what is around us (this made me question which layers evolution has actually taken place).\nIt seems that there are millions of people around the world who appear to have been mentally \

, where they have lost the ability to think for themselves. Not only that (which is already a lot, obviously), but they have also lost the ability to question. The creativity of thinking outside the box seems to have been thrown down the drain, along with the ability to hone (and refine) one's own mind and all its strong intellect.\nThese millions of people reinforce my thinking about how the art of thinking (which is one of the sensitive and most easily visible aspects that differentiate us from other types of animals) has been lost over the years, at an increasingly rapid pace, as more people discover new ways to \

what another part of society thinks, and how that same group should act. Could this be the battle humanistically lost?
---
<center>**¿Se ha perdido el arte de pensar?**</center>
Cuando hablamos de evolución humana, quien se atreva a cuestionarlo demuestra una inmensa estupidez e ignorancia. En efecto, la evolución humana ha ocurrido. Sin embargo, es necesario prestar atención a otro punto: ¿hasta dónde ha llegado esta evolución tras tantos años? Sé que no existen respuestas definitivas, pero no está de más “cavar” para comprender dónde nos encontramos.
Este texto me vino a la mente (hace poco) tras ver un anuncio de televisión sobre el poder de los influencers digitales en la sociedad actual. El anuncio no se centraba en cómo lo hacen, sino en invitar al espectador a reflexionar sobre el arte de pensar mediante el pensamiento crítico sobre nuestro entorno (esto me hizo preguntarme en qué niveles de evolución se ha producido realmente).
Parece que millones de personas en todo el mundo se han “submergido” mentalmente en una especie de \

, donde han perdido la capacidad de pensar por sí mismas. Y no solo eso (que ya es mucho, obviamente), sino que también han perdido la capacidad de cuestionar. La creatividad de pensar de forma innovadora parece haberse esfumado, junto con la capacidad de cultivar (y refinar) la propia mente y todo su intelecto.\nEstos millones de personas refuerzan mi idea de cómo el arte de pensar (uno de los aspectos más sensibles y visibles que nos diferencian de otros animales) se ha ido perdiendo con el paso de los años, a un ritmo cada vez mayor, a medida que más personas descubren nuevas formas de \

lo que piensa otra parte de la sociedad y cómo debería actuar ese mismo grupo. ¿Podría ser esta la batalla perdida desde el punto de vista humanista? ---
**A arte de pensar foi perdida?**
Quando falamos sobre evolução humana, qualquer pessoa que tenha a audácia de questionar esse fato está assinando um atestado de estupidez e ignorância sem tamanho. De fato, a evolução humana aconteceu. No entanto, é preciso se atentar um outro ponto: até onde essa evolução conseguiu chegar depois de tantos anos? Eu sei que respostas efetivas sobre isso não podem ser encontradas em nenhum lugar, mas não faz mal algum “cavar” para entender onde estamos. Esse texto me veio precisamente a mente (mais cedo) depois que eu assisti um comercial na televisão falando sobre o poder que os influencers digitais dentro da sociedade atual. O foco do comercial não era, no entanto, falar sobre como os influencers digitais fazem isso; mas sim, provocar o telespectador sobre a arte de pensar através de um pensamento crítico sobre o que está ao nosso redor (isso me fez questionar sobre quais camadas a evolução realmente aconteceu). Ao que parece, há milhões de pessoas mundo à fora que parecem ter sido mentalmente “absorvidas” para uma espécie de “realidade paralela”, onde elas perderam a capacidade de pensar por elas mesmas. Não apenas isso (que já é muita coisa, obviamente), mas também, perderam a capacidade de questionar. A criatividade de pensar fora da caixa parece que foi jogada no ralo, juntamente com a habilidade de lapidar (e refinar) a própria mente e todo o seu forte intelecto. Esses milhões de pessoas reforçam o meu pensamento sobre como a arte de pensar (que é um dos aspectos sensíveis e mais facilmente visíveis que nos diferem dos outros tipos de animais) vem sendo perdida ao longo dos anos, em um ritmo cada vez mais rápido, à medida em que mais pessoas vão descobrindo novas maneiras de “controlar” o que uma outra parte da sociedade pensa, e como esse mesmo grupo deve agir. Seria essa a batalha humanisticamente perdida? Posted Using [INLEO](https://inleo.io/@wiseagent/has-the-art-of-thinking-been-lost)

links.title: The Big Short Is One of the Smartest Financial Films Ever Made. It Takes a Complicated Real World Disaster and Somehow Makes It Entertaining, Educational, and Infuriating at the Same Time.
links.body:
More Than Just a Great Movie, The Big Short Tells the True Story of a Handful of Investors Who Saw the 2008 Financial Collapse Coming Long Before Anyone Else. Their Story Is Fascinating, and the Film Does an Outstanding Job Bringing It to Life.

![IMG_2586.webp](https://images.hive.blog/DQmSxdJicPYpa9pRF9EZcs3RfBvwCfeRsESH5fG17a64Mp4/IMG_2586.webp)

Released in 2015, The Big Short is one of those rare films that manages to be both incredibly entertaining and incredibly important. Directed by Adam McKay, the movie tackles the complicated events that led to the 2008 financial crisis, a disaster that devastated millions of people around the world. What makes the film so impressive is that it takes a subject many people find confusing and turns it into a gripping story.

The film is based on the nonfiction book by Michael Lewis and follows several real life investors and financial experts who noticed serious problems in the American housing market years before the crash happened. While most banks, investors, government officials, and financial media personalities believed everything was fine, a small group of outsiders saw a disaster approaching.

Christian Bale delivers one of the best performances in the film as Dr. Michael Burry, a brilliant but socially awkward hedge fund manager who begins examining mortgage data and discovers that the entire housing market is built on a foundation of risky loans. Bale completely disappears into the role and makes Burry one of the most fascinating characters in the movie.

Steve Carell is equally impressive as Mark Baum, a character based on real life investor Steve Eisman. Baum is angry, cynical, and deeply frustrated by the corruption he uncovers. Carell gives the film much of its emotional weight, as his character struggles with the realization that the financial system is far more broken than he ever imagined.

Ryan Gosling plays Jared Vennett, a fast talking banker who recognizes the opportunity created by Burry’s discovery. Gosling serves as a narrator throughout much of the film and brings a lot of energy and humor to what could have been a very dry subject.

Brad Pitt also delivers a strong performance as Ben Rickert, a retired trader who helps two young investors navigate the complicated world of Wall Street. Pitt’s character provides an important reminder that while some people stood to make enormous profits, the coming crash would have devastating consequences for ordinary families.

The plot centers around these different individuals as they independently discover that millions of risky mortgages have been bundled together and sold as safe investments. Realizing that the housing bubble is eventually going to collapse, they make enormous bets against the market. In other words, they are betting that the system will fail.

One of the most fascinating parts of the movie is watching these men become increasingly frustrated as nobody wants to listen to them. Banks dismiss them. Rating agencies ignore obvious problems. Financial experts insist everything is fine. The deeper they dig, the more unbelievable the situation becomes.

Adam McKay deserves tremendous credit for making such a complicated topic understandable. The film uses humor, celebrity cameos, and creative fourth wall breaks to explain complicated financial concepts. Normally these techniques might feel gimmicky, but here they work perfectly.

What makes The Big Short especially powerful is that it is a true story. The events actually happened. The corruption, the greed, the incompetence, and the complete failure of oversight were all real. Watching the film knowing this makes many scenes even more shocking.

The movie never portrays its main characters as traditional heroes. While they correctly predicted the crash, they also profited from it. That creates an interesting moral dilemma throughout the film. The audience wants them to be right, but at the same time knows that being right means millions of people will suffer.

Visually, the film moves at a fast pace and never becomes boring despite dealing with economics and finance. The editing is sharp, the performances are excellent, and the script constantly balances humor with outrage.

What I love most about The Big Short is that it exposes how fragile and reckless the financial system had become before 2008. It shows how a handful of intelligent people were willing to question what everyone else accepted as fact, and how that willingness allowed them to see the truth long before the rest of the world.

![IMG_2585.webp](https://images.hive.blog/DQmQQnS17PMTxYTYiBZq3eyDoWzKY2BbtN6KGH1RCwRsJx3/IMG_2585.webp)

The Big Short remains a great film because it succeeds on multiple levels. It is entertaining, informative, funny, frustrating, and at times genuinely shocking. More importantly, it tells a true story that everyone should understand. It is one of the best films ever made about finance and one of the most compelling true stories Hollywood has brought to the screen.

links.title: 喻世明言十一《沈小官一鸟害七命》
links.body:
一鸟害七命沈小官一鸟害七命，今天就来捋一捋这7条人命都是谁。
一：第一条人命当然就是沈小官沈秀，他自己在树林子里疝气发作，小腹疼痛昏迷，箍桶匠张公谋鸟害命，把他给杀了。树人头给扔在旁边的树洞里面了。
二：命案发了，凶手像人间蒸发了一样，寻不得。沈秀父母只得寻一个全尸来安葬。然后寻全尸的过程中就发生了那个黄姓老儿，穷的一家三口儿都揭不开锅的那么一家人，穷生奸计嘛，就告诉他两个儿子，说如今沈老板家要寻一个全尸，还给赏钱，我又老又没用，你们赶紧把我的头给拿去领赏，别去晚了，让别人儿先领了赏了我就白死了。
所以说，生孩子嘛，还得生两个，商量拔管子时也得有一个拿主意的人。
这两个儿子就在门外一合计，老爹也老了，也没什么用了，还不如拿去换点儿钱，又是他自己出的馊主意，跟我们没有关系。

![](https://i.ecency.com/DQmQ1fqPTNRsAHZd5NU3jqohHkn6NG4j92zcxTUcCFtFR3R/img_3025.jpg)

小儿子于心不忍，这毕竟是爹呀！大儿子拍个板儿说，反正是他自己要死的，跟我们没有关系，还不如拿他的头换点儿钱，给我们尽最后一点儿余力呢。就这么滴，两个就把老爹的头拿去领了赏了。
这也真下得去手！
三：这是第二条命了，这第三条命呢，话说这个真凶张公把鸟儿夺去之后，就卖给了一个叫李吉的东京的商人，这个商人就觉得这个鸟儿太好了，不舍得自己用，就给进贡了。

世界还是真是太小。
沈老板家因为儿子的全尸也有了，入了棺了，时间久了沈老板和这个官府也都不想着抓凶手了。

过了好久，轮到沈老板押解缎匹贡品到东京，干完工作之后，他觉得这个首都里面的风光听说跟别处不一样啊，好不容易来一趟，咱就去逛一逛吧。

他就逛山逛水逛庙宇，一天他逛到禽鸟馆，他也是爱那些禽鸟的，所以说啊，从心理学上来说，他儿子的行为就是在满足他父母的被压抑的那些爱好、想法，孩子就是父母的镜子。

就像是学霸生了个学渣的孩子一样，虽然他们是学霸，但是他们内心里是厌恶学习的，孩子就是他们的镜子，就走了他们真正的那条厌学之路。

这沈老板的儿子也就是走了沈老板那个被压抑的天性，成天就斗个画眉，用世人的眼光来说，就是不务正业。那其实是他父亲的没有被实现的一个信念。

未完待续……

***

![](https://images.ecency.com/DQmdH5Dnw8LqqcdpG4x6RtEttfbwL3y7sHLmqxpDVfCDriX/img_5677.gif)

links.title: A's lose to Yankees 13-8 | They're in Chicago tonight with Gage Jump on the mound for second MLB start
links.body:
Yeah late post since I got caught up in the most pointless thing of all time. Ugh. Super annoying. Thank God for sports man. 

The A's got basically crushed the other day against the Yankees. It was kinda historic as the Yankees scored thirteen runs in an inning. It was pretty rough. Luckily I'm used to stress and suffering as a sports fan and in life LOL. It was actually pretty funny honestly. What else can I do but laugh at such a wild experience. It's rare at the end of the day. 

In fact, it was *almost* a more wild game as the A's sorta made it interesting and sorta kinda threatened to come back! I pictured how glorious that would have been and got a bit excited, but it wasn't meant to be. 

Jacob Lopez once again had a bad start as I feared he would. He actually got send to Triple-A after the game. I wasn't as harsh as I feared I was being regarding his play, he was pitching pretty poorly consistently! Hopefully he can reset and find a groove in the minors and return eventually. 

But now the A's have two pitchers on the IL and one sent down. Yikes!!

links.title: The Street Never Passes by in Blank -  B&W PHOTOGRAPHY - from São Paulo - Brasil II ENG - PT_BR II ( 09 Shots )
links.body:
![TEMPLATE ART ALIEN HIVE.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/grafvisionsp/48XfYHXE1YHrg325kwPjvYhKtLbpNAQvKtTC5cS7dXC2kYmn8qoKuWZ7cT1S178yGu.jpg)








Once again, I bring you these street photography shots, showing a little more of my obsession with capturing everyday life. Wherever I go, there's always that urge to stop for a few seconds and transform an ordinary moment into a memory. It's almost an addiction, a constant need to observe and preserve what my eyes find along the way. A gaze that can't ignore the details, the simple scenes, the people going about their business, the architecture worn by time, and everything that normally goes unnoticed in the rush of daily life.





> Novamente trago a vocês esses disparos de fotografia de rua, mostrando mais um pouco dessa minha sina por registrar o cotidiano. Por onde eu passo, existe sempre aquela vontade de parar por alguns segundos e transformar um instante comum em memória. É quase um vício, uma necessidade constante de observar e guardar aquilo que os olhos encontram pelo caminho. Um olhar que não consegue ignorar os detalhes, as cenas simples, as pessoas seguindo seus caminhos, a arquitetura desgastada pelo tempo e tudo aquilo que normalmente passa despercebido na correria do dia a dia.
------------------------













![_MG_3248PB.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/grafvisionsp/2423sZYuguo6nQvGw7rb1FudJmFc7PRiSXQKDsw8ByLAdXT11aTdu7ozHMehVPwnKBEKj.jpg)











📷 **01.** / Canon EOS 60D




















![meninos bola.png](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/grafvisionsp/23w2mG5qAFzeGeCSKbqA3FHNkCCSPbnMsxjvZVnVhjgrWNjHGe4L9sTs1nwBZcPAXuX2f.png)





📷 **02.**  / Canon EOS 60D




------------------------

I often go out without a specific destination, just walking the streets, observing the city's movement and waiting for something to happen in front of the lens. And it almost always does. It might be an unexpected reflection in a shop window, a shadow cast by the late afternoon light, a lost expression in the crowd, or even a moment of silence on a busy street. These are moments that last only a few seconds, but carry entire stories within them.



> Muitas vezes saio sem destino definido, apenas caminhando pelas ruas, observando o movimento da cidade e esperando que algo aconteça diante da lente. E quase sempre acontece. Pode ser um reflexo inesperado em uma vitrine, uma sombra desenhada pela luz do fim da tarde, uma expressão perdida em meio à multidão ou até mesmo um instante de silêncio em uma rua movimentada. São momentos que duram apenas alguns segundos, mas que carregam histórias inteiras dentro deles.
-----------------------

















![_MG_3297PB.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/grafvisionsp/23w2iyTNYg6huRKT27u3VNZ9KLKp4sTjf9VLxLn7YBhjDJY6NLkbNf8Aprj2VD6ZcXcdq.jpg)






📷 **03.**  / Canon EOS 60D























![_MG_3343PB.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/grafvisionsp/23wC9vTQg2BtbeTVE4auaXsgG6ZPTTEYbCFcfVrkjbhe4BKhHTfuzCbPYeTBpypWXigME.jpg)





📷 **04.**  / Canon EOS 60D




















![_MG_3351PB.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/grafvisionsp/23z7Bq9ouuD93yW1J1acY6joQBcvE1aMgZgpkGGuzoifSSRBaUjYBDsDzfRHHrFZ3hbrY.jpg)




📷 **05.**  / Canon EOS 60D




------------------------

The street always has something to say. It changes its face at every corner, with every light that shines through the buildings, with every character that enters and exits the scene without even imagining that they are part of a larger story. Perhaps it is precisely this unpredictability that makes me continue photographing. I never know exactly what I will find, and this uncertainty makes each walk a new discovery. The desire to find beauty in the ordinary, to see poetry where many people see only routine, is what drives me to continue.



> A rua sempre tem algo a dizer. Ela muda de rosto a cada esquina, a cada luz que atravessa os prédios, a cada personagem que entra e sai de cena sem nem imaginar que faz parte de uma história maior. Talvez seja justamente essa imprevisibilidade que me faça continuar fotografando. Nunca sei exatamente o que vou encontrar, e essa incerteza torna cada caminhada uma nova descoberta. A vontade de encontrar beleza no comum, de enxergar poesia onde muita gente vê apenas rotina, é o que me impulsiona a continuar.
------------------------














![_MG_3356PB.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/grafvisionsp/23uFZw9CgPRb6YpnvbgDZceN2mQxSzraNdAKdpDGpTunKCvKBNm6gNtyokxiMkiQL4DTA.jpg)



📷 **06.**  / Canon EOS 60D





There's something fascinating about how the city transforms throughout the day. In the morning, everything seems to rush by, with people going to work and trying to beat the clock. In the afternoon, the light changes, contrasts appear, and new scenes unfold before your eyes. As night falls, the streets take on a different atmosphere, illuminated by lampposts, shop windows, and headlights, creating completely different scenarios from those seen a few hours earlier. Each moment offers a new opportunity for observation and recording.


> Existe algo fascinante na forma como a cidade se transforma ao longo do dia. Pela manhã, tudo parece correr em um ritmo acelerado, com pessoas indo ao trabalho e tentando vencer o relógio. À tarde, a luz muda, os contrastes aparecem e novas cenas surgem diante dos olhos. Já ao anoitecer, as ruas ganham outra atmosfera, iluminadas por postes, vitrines e faróis, criando cenários completamente diferentes daqueles vistos algumas horas antes. Cada momento oferece uma nova oportunidade de observação e registro.











![_MG_3370PB.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/grafvisionsp/23xAiMjKkaAq6DkEWggEXxbWJbpmgDXUo4swLvADUfjbnsgjYqRz4WT3H5abXgG4hHY4B.jpg)



📷 **07.**  / Canon EOS 60D






















![_MG_3379.JPG](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/grafvisionsp/23tSMiSNEKYCxnDD5JDHvANuqmdkbRuHBJMXRPsdFWRCbWmTSEJwkpej5NTSkq1mVeGce.JPG)








📷 **08.**  / Canon EOS 60D





------------------------
These images are fragments of the paths I travel, records of fleeting encounters between my gaze and the moment. There is no script, no direction. Just the street being itself, alive, chaotic, silent at times, noisy at others, but always full of stories waiting to be perceived. Each photograph represents a small pause in the constant flow of the city, an attempt to freeze something that, in the next second, will no longer be the same.



> Essas imagens são fragmentos dos caminhos que percorro, registros de encontros rápidos entre o olhar e o momento. Não existe roteiro, não existe direção. Apenas a rua sendo ela mesma, viva, caótica, silenciosa às vezes, barulhenta em outras, mas sempre cheia de histórias esperando para serem percebidas. Cada fotografia representa uma pequena pausa no fluxo constante da cidade, uma tentativa de congelar algo que, no segundo seguinte, já não será mais o mesmo.

------------------------


















![_MG_3727pb.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/grafvisionsp/23wWtfkCQCLerjcGrw6pkdsfummHQNMHjLzVPjL7UtmAoyc5e2UFz2ATFWEm5t1NwjN3z.jpg)







📷 **09.** / Canon EOS 60D


------------------------


What fascinates me most about street photography is precisely this ability to reveal the extraordinary hidden within the ordinary. Often, what seems banal at first glance takes on a new meaning when observed more closely. A simple gesture, a distant gaze, a combination of colors, or an everyday scene can transform into something special when captured at the right moment.

> O que mais me encanta na fotografia de rua é justamente essa capacidade de revelar o extraordinário escondido dentro do ordinário. Muitas vezes, aquilo que parece banal à primeira vista ganha um novo significado quando observado com mais atenção. Um gesto simples, um olhar distante, uma combinação de cores ou uma cena cotidiana podem se transformar em algo especial quando registrados no momento certo.










------------------------



As I walk these streets, I believe this urge to document will hardly ever go away. Because for me, photography is much more than simply producing images. It's a way of staying attentive to the world, of creating connections with places and people I may never see again, but who, for a fraction of a second, were part of the same landscape and the same moment.



> Enquanto eu caminhar por essas ruas, acredito que essa vontade de registrar dificilmente vai embora. Porque fotografar, para mim, é muito mais do que simplesmente produzir imagens. É uma forma de permanecer atento ao mundo, de criar conexões com lugares e pessoas que talvez eu nunca mais encontre, mas que por uma fração de segundo fizeram parte da mesma paisagem e do mesmo instante.
------------------------








------------------------

links.title: Miri to Bintulu
links.body: Good Morning to all my wonderful friends here @asean.hive How has your week been? It's a Wednesday. I recently went on a trip to Bintulu, which is around two and a half hours from Miri. The road to Bintulu is superbly great. The government of Sarawak has done a good job of building the Pan Borneo Highway. It used to take around 3 and a half to 4 hours to arrive in Bintulu from Miri due to small roads, but now, after the highway has been built, it has made travelling much easier. The sky is amazing. The special thing about this highway is that no toll is collected, so smooth journey from one district to another.
/> The amazing drive. I enjoy driving from time to time as a getaway from the daily hustle and bustle. The one thing to do in Bintulu is just to enjoy the food there.

/> This is what the journey looks like on Google Maps. There are two straight roads from one city to another. The older coastal road is only a one-lane road. So, it takes a bit longer to reach Bintulu. So, I chose the Highway. Miri is located on very near to the sea so all along the way as you are driving, the view of the sea is never out of sight.
/> After a bit of driving, I reached at around evening. The first stop is food. I went to Sharing @Bintulu This is also one of those cities here in Malaysia that has the highest GDP per capita.

/> This restaurant is famous for Western Inspired food like Chicken Chop, Fish and chips to name a few. There are many restaurants that serve Western Food In Bintulu. This is the menu and the prices of the food. 1 USD = RM 3.96
/> The nice ambience inside. This is the aircon section, and the aircon is cold. A really nice place for you to hang out with your family or just to hang out.
/> We sat at table 27. There are a lot tables available.
/> FISH AND CHIPS ============== Instead of having fries, we had mashed potatoes. Tartar sauce.

/> The fish they used is not a Dory fish, which is what is commonly found in the supermarket. I was shocked at how big their fried chicken chop was. This is one huge fish. Amazing. It comes with fries too.
/> The macaroni It is truly delicious. The gravy is mixed well and it blends well with the macaroni inside.
/> Thank you very much for reading this post. Overall, the food here is delicious. The ambience here is amazing. @luueetang YouTube: www.youtube.com/luueejanice Tiktok: www.tiktok.com/@luueejanice

If you're on Peakd, our favourite interface for the Hive blockchain, simply click on this link for the [Ocean Lover's community](https://peakd.com/c/hive-120883/created). I've been MIA because I've been very busy, but I'm back again. A week ago, I had a bad case of the flu and a fever, so I took medicine and got better quickly. Today, I felt like I had the flu again. My body probably needed a break. It's been a lot of work and walking these past few weeks, so I took a break and had some coconut water. They say it's good for you and refreshing. I hope to feel much better tomorrow and eat better, haha. This was a summary of my day. Bye.

links.title: Are you actually building yourself?
links.body:
![IMG_20240914_121551_652~3-1.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/chizzy100/242No5dd6QRwABkRGsjkRKuxjqfsUKvsgcrS6BNbMVJRU2KYkEBWoGP2yvi4CW4eokak9.jpg)
Everybody wants growth until growth starts demanding change.

When I first entered the media space in 2023, I started with CorelDRAW. Thankfully, I was given a fairly used, old HP laptop that was originally a desktop... Do you get? No battery.

But at that stage, I was just grateful to have something to learn with. After a while, I moved into web design and started learning coding.
Guess what happened?

The system couldn’t even install Visual Studio Code. That was when reality hit me hard: what helped me start couldn’t carry me to the next level.

Later on, I got another fairly used HP laptop.

Still not strong enough for the kind of work I wanted to do at the time — graphics, coding, design… everything was stressing the system and stressing me too. 

Six months later, I switched fully into design and I couldn’t cope anymore. Guess what I bought next? Not a system, a phone!

This is exactly how growth works sometimes.

![IMG_5188~2_1.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/chizzy100/23ynWJwYiDsi1mo6GzidVcGicEKV4wvNkqHBvcLWmpbisfGVKXUfpSY3pLtDdLGB4espH.jpg)

Every new level demands a change.
Your mind naturally starts craving what matches where you’re trying to go.

Sometimes it’s your environment.Sometimes it’s your circle.Sometimes it’s your mindset, your relationships, your tools, your habits… something always has to change.

People who truly want growth don’t stay stuck doing life one way forever.

So the moment you start feeling uncomfortable with where you are, or you begin desiring more for yourself, don’t ignore it. That discomfort might actually be growth calling you. 

The real question is:
Will you answer?
This thought came to me this morning and I thought to share. 

As we step into a new month, take a moment to pause and check yourself. 

Not your likes, comments, or the applause from social media.

YOU!

Here are a few things to evaluate:

What new skill have you learned since January?

What course or training have you invested in?

What habit have you developed that is making you better?
What bad habit have you intentionally worked on breaking?

Are you more disciplined today than you were at the beginning of the year?

What have you built, started, or completed in the last five months?

Who are the people pouring into your growth?

![Screenshot_20240914-160410.png](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/chizzy100/23vhuW18XQRm4PjA2ZFQKcvMes1v9SiCJCQ7mXC6M6ZKgBksW9eF42m3WLMW8yuvLNNNL.png)

How have you invested in your personal, and professional development? If someone met you today and met you in January, would they notice any growth?

• Are you becoming the person you prayed to be?

Sometimes, people say, \

But inspiration is not the same as growth.

Take a moment today.

Sit with your thoughts.

Review your year so far and be brutally honest with yourself.

Are you actually building yourself?

I'm not exempted from this message too.
Remember when we were told that a university degree was the golden ticket to a secure life?

Yeah, times changed.

The reality hitting graduates today is brutal: you spend four to five years memorizing textbooks, walk across the stage in your gown, and step straight into a job market that speaks a completely different language.

There is a dangerous, gaping chasm between what universities teach and what the modern workforce actually demands.

Right now, the internet is the new oil and gas waiting to be tapped by young creatives, adults, and teenagers alike. But you can't drill for oil with a shovel. You need the right tools.

And today, that tool is AI and Creativity:

If you’re a student, you must learn how AI applies to your specific craft.
 
![IMG_1784.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/chizzy100/23zkta4J3gQ1FhKhW62PgnKcJ8oUbtpTRWDUQxkiPtGbHYdoiZkHCk6GDYssq355iL8dA.jpg)

If you're a writer, learn AI prompting for research.
If you're a designer, learn AI-driven ideation.
If you're a marketer, learn AI data analytics.

Don't let a rigid curriculum dictate your future potential. School gives you a foundation, but the internet gives you the toolkit. USE IT!

What's one digital skill you're betting on this year?
Say in the comment. 
All images are mine.
